title: Nurses’ Knowledge, Clinical Practices, and Structural Barriers in Hospital Fall Prevention: A Cross-Sectional Study in Albania
content: Background: Patient falls are among the most frequent and significant adverse events in hospital settings, directly affecting patient safety and increasing hospital stays and healthcare costs. Falls from the bed are particularly problematic as they occur within an environment geared toward recovery—one that is expected to be highly controlled and safe. This study aimed to identify risk factors contributing to inpatient falls, assess baseline clinical knowledge, and analyze nurses’ pivotal role in fall prevention through systematic assessment and preventive interventions, while also identifying structural barriers. Materials and Methods: This was a quantitative, descriptive, cross-sectional study. Data were collected using a structured 13-item questionnaire designed to evaluate the knowledge, clinical practices, and preventive measures implemented by nursing staff regarding hospital falls. The study involved the voluntary participation of 52 nurses from various clinical hospital departments. Data were collected anonymously, strictly adhering to ethical principles of confidentiality; nurses were informed of and retained the right to withdraw at any stage of the research. The instrument covered variables regarding demographic data, clinical knowledge of predisposing risk factors, the use of standardized assessment tools, and current safety practices. Results and Discussion: The data indicated that nursing staff possess good theoretical knowledge regarding fall-related risk factors and safety measures. The majority of participants emphasized the critical importance of early risk identification and continuous daily monitoring. However, a significant procedural gap was identified: 48.1% of departments do not use any structured fall assessment scale, and 50.0% of nurses are not fully aware of their institution’s approved tool. High workload (42.3%) and acute staff shortages (40.4%) were reported as major operational barriers. The results indicate that preventing patient falls is inextricably linked to addressing structural human resource limitations and reinforcing strict adherence to standard safety procedures. Conclusions: Patient falls in hospitals remain a critical challenge within healthcare delivery systems. Enhancing continuous nursing education, optimizing clinical nurse-to-patient ratios, and implementing mandatory, institutionalized prevention protocols are paramount to minimizing risks and ensuring high-quality patient safety.
